🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.35% (intraday, 7-year +19bp). At trading day 16 (last close) it was -1.11% against a five-campaign average of -1.01% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.28%. The 10-year is +23bp since the hike vs a +13bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 719bp against a five-year average of 410bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +38bp and BB +35bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.21 → 0.52 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+2bp).
  • Stocks: US futures point higher after Thursday's tech-led drop; Europe is up strongly.
  • FX: The dollar is a touch firmer; the euro is below its long-run trend; the yen is still weak.
  • Technicals: US stocks sit well above their long-run trend and look stretched; history gives roughly even odds of a turn.
  • Sectors: Energy and staples led while tech lagged, a defensive-and-commodity tilt.
  • Credit/Spreads: Most corporate bonds still pay little extra yield, but the riskiest junk is under real strain.

The pre-market tone is constructive. ES is +24.75 at 7841.0 (+0.3166480089557013%) and NQ is +227.5 at 31197.0 (+0.7345937131694087%), so the futures are partly reversing Thursday's tech-led drop. In that session the S&P 500 fell 36.41 points to 7765.36 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 345.35 to 27193.34, while the Dow (+51.77) and Russell 2000 (+0.924) were flat to slightly higher. Europe is helping: Euro Stoxx 50 +70.32 to 6197.05, STOXX 600 +7.14 to 632.65 and FTSE 100 +113.4 to 10555.0. The VIX is 15.17 (from 15.41). Two things undercut the bounce. First, US Treasuries are selling off again: the 2Y is up 4.61bp to 4.8038%, the 10Y up 3.22bp to 5.259% and the 30Y up 2.29bp to 5.623%, while Bund, Gilt and JGB yields all fall. That makes this a US-specific rates story, tied to the Fed's September hike and a deficit of -5.441% of GDP. Second, and the biggest story under the surface, the lowest-rated junk bonds are under worsening stress. The Caa–B spread gap is 719bp, at the 100th percentile of its 5-year history (5y avg ~410bp). It widened +97bp in a month and +204bp in three months, and Caa OAS at 1014bp is the widest since April 2020. Is it spreading? Partly. Over the past month single-B widened +38bp and Ba +35bp, but both tightened last week (-15bp and -6bp). The B–Ba gap is only 106bp (31st 5y percentile), and IG is barely changed at 81bp (+2bp in 1m). The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has risen to 0.52 from 0.28 a month ago and 0.21 three months ago, still below its 0.70 5-year median. So the CCC rot has nudged the rest of high yield wider, but it has not broken out into single-B, BB or investment grade. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Commodities are mixed: Brent is -1.16 to 103.12 and WTI -0.65 to 90.84, while gold (+49.22 to 4181.72), silver and copper rally. The Iran war has no ceasefire, but Washington has shifted to sanctions and pledged no new strikes before the Nov 3 midterms, which helps explain the softer oil. Sentiment: cautiously risk-on in stocks, risk-off in long US bonds and the weakest credits.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

US 1-day: Energy (+2.92) and Cons Staples (+2.12) led, with Financials (+0.91) next. Info Tech (-1.78) lagged most, followed by Cons Discr (-0.47) and Health Care (-0.41). That is a classic defensive-plus-inflation-hedge rotation away from growth. The 1-week window agrees: Energy and Staples (+4.03 each) and Utilities (+3.48) lead, while Tech (+0.44) and Industrials (-0.13) trail. Over 1 month Tech (+5.21) and Comm Services (+4.47) still lead, while rate-sensitive Real Estate (-5.53), Financials (-4.71), Utilities (-3.83) and Materials (-3.31) lag, which fits a 5%+ 10-year yield. YTD, Energy (+42.73) and Tech (+29.32) dominate a barbell, while Cons Discr (-2.7), Utilities (-4.97) and Financials (-1.23) are negative. Globally the picture is similar: Energy (+2.58) and Staples (+1.57) led, and Tech (-1.7) lagged on the day. Global Materials (-7.68) and Financials and Real Estate (-5.96 each) have been hit harder over 1 month, a sign that higher global rates and a strong dollar are biting outside the US. Net: value and defensives are gaining at the margin, but the 1-month window shows growth leadership is dented, not broken.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.97 vol points (71th percentile of the 38 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 100.7 (73th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 108bp (steeper by 31bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20

Right rim5.30%2026-10-05

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (90bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 8 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Core inflation trends are cooling, but headline/flexible prices and breadth remain hot because of the oil shock. Persistence is moderate, and the risk tilts toward stickiness while Brent stays above $100. The computed core-trend measures all point lower (median CPI 2.58, trimmed-mean CPI 2.57, median PCE 2.57, trimmed-mean PCE 2.19, core sticky CPI 2.7, all 'falling'), sitting near their historical middle. But flexible CPI at 4.94 and the Dallas distribution, with 13.2% of the PCE basket inflating above 10% and 15.7% at 5-10% (about 29% above 5%), show the energy shock is broad. Core PCE YoY at 3.00759 is still well above target, and 1y breakevens (2.7915) above 5y (2.3772) say markets see a temporary hump, not de-anchoring. Wage pressure is muted (AHE 3.0, ECI 0.9), so a wage-price spiral is not in evidence. That makes the Fed's hawkishness a credibility choice more than a labor-market necessity.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (44x) ≈ 25% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

On the 1990-anchored path chart (computed), the current cycle (Oct-2022 anchor) is at month 48 with an index value of 247.5. That is close to where the 1990s bull stood at the same age (235.7), and it peaked only at month 113 (1423.9). On the analog alone, there could be years of runway, not months. The analyst-estimate gauges add context. S&P top-10 concentration is around 35% (June 2026 Motley Fool). The Shiller CAPE is around 41, near its 44.19 dot-com high. The Buffett ratio is about 237% of GDP (September 2026 reports). Long-term EPS-growth expectations look elevated, though below 2000 extremes (65/100). IPO froth is moderate (45/100): a handful of mega-deals (Anthropic, Jio) are queued, but this week's US calendar is small-cap biotech, not the 2000-style flood. The part of today's setup that rhymes most with 2000 is not the Nasdaq multiple. It is complacent credit and volatility sitting next to a Fed that is tightening into a supply shock. Watch whether CCC stress moves up into single-B and IG, the late-cycle catalyst that is still missing.

⚔️Iran War

No ceasefire is in force, and the war is in a tense, stalled phase. Diplomacy: talks are at an impasse after President Trump rejected Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Iran says it is reviewing the US response and preparing its own, with Pakistan, Oman, Qatar and Egypt mediating (CBS). Military: Trump has pledged no US strikes on Iran before the Nov 3 midterms, and Washington has shifted toward economic pressure (CBS). On Thursday Treasury sanctioned what it called 'the remnants of Iran's shadow fleet,' saying the action 'effectively neutralizes the vast majority' of the network (CBS). Hormuz: trackers report the strait remains closed by Iranian declaration and traffic is at a two-month low. Iran and Oman have agreed coordinates for safe-transit routes, while tanker attacks are reportedly at their highest weekly level of the war (Iran War Live tracker; unverified tracker data). 🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Analyst estimate (inferred): a hawkish lean at the next FOMC, with another 25bp hike to 4.00-4.25% somewhat more likely than a hold. Basis: on Sept 16 Warsh said the economy strengthened, inflation did not slow and financial conditions had loosened, and that inflation is the top priority. The 2Y at 4.8038%, well above the 3.75-4.00% funds range, implies markets expect more tightening (inference). A hold is plausible given weak payrolls (29k) and cooling core-trend measures. He said he is 'not in the forward guidance business,' so expect data dependence.

~1 YEAR

Analyst estimate (inferred): a cumulative 50-75bp of further tightening over roughly 12 months if oil keeps headline inflation hot, then a long hold. Core-trend measures already near historical norms argue for a short cycle. Political friction with the White House is likely to persist. Inference: Warsh's long-standing criticism of a large Fed balance sheet suggests he may also favor continued runoff, but this run's search did not verify that, so it is flagged as unconfirmed.

At his Aug 28 Jackson Hole speech Warsh signaled that stubborn inflation might require hikes, saying recent reports did not show underlying trends had meaningfully improved (PBS). On Sept 16 the FOMC voted 12-0 to raise rates 25bp to 3.75-4.00%, the first hike since 2023. Warsh framed it as removing 'a dose of accommodation' and stressed that inflation is the priority (CNN, CNBC, Fed transcript). He also said the Fed cannot fix shipping-lane disruption or 'affect any individual price' such as oil or groceries (Fed transcript). CNBC noted markets are pricing several more hikes. Warsh has also publicly pushed back on Trump's rate criticism (Yahoo Finance). Our near-term and one-year calls are inferences from these statements, not guidance.
